So the strength was too low for First, and this pass can't judge the register properly. First won on only 42 of 256 prompts (16%), and those were a selected group. The 42 show 19.0% accuracy against 26.2% for the original on the same problems, which is noise at that size and certainly not encouraging. The style itself is what I expected: "First, we need to find ...", then plain sentences with short equations. There's also a side effect: 10 answers flipped from Let to Here, so the Let-Here counter-write overshoots for this direction. That drift was specific to We, so I'll halve the correction.

Getting First to dominate needs about 2-3 more logits, and near the RMS ceiling that would take a much larger write, so it would need a second write site. Okay should be easier and needs no new tool, since its gap is only about -8. I'll test it next at 1.7 times its base strength, on the same problems, under the same bar. If Okay dominates and doesn't beat E5's 23.9% by about 3 points, then four styles will have been tried, and I'll have to ask whether a second site for First is worth building at all. Conversational registers often run longer, so I'll also watch cut-offs.

E9 is saved and in the notes, with a smaller write than for First (|dy|/|ymean| 0.73), because Okay starts closer. I'll run the paired generation pass on `dev_a1`. The opener share comes first this time: the register test only counts if Okay wins on most prompts, and if it does, I'll compare accuracy with E5's 23.9% on these same problems.

This one looks different. Overall accuracy is about flat at -0.4 ± 2.4, but cut-offs fall a lot, from 27.0% to 19.9%, and mean length drops from 345 to 297 tokens. If most answers opened with Okay, that's a register with fewer loops but also more wrong finishes. I need the opener split before I can read that.

I'll use the same breakdown as before: opener counts, the Okay group against the original and E5, results by natural opener and by margin, and a short reading of the style. The interesting question is where any accuracy gain sits. If Okay does better than Here on natural-Here problems but worse than Let on natural-Let problems, then in principle it could replace Here in a mixed policy, as Let does in E5. It would only add value if it beats Let on those flipped problems. The method says to judge by accuracy, so the cut-off drop doesn't count for anything by itself.

Okay won on 198 of 256 prompts, and every one of the 117 natural-Here problems moved, so this is a fair test. Its style turns out to be the markdown list family, "Okay, let's break down the problem step-by-step: 1. **Calculate ...**", much like "Here's". Overall it fails the bar, at 22.3% against E5's 23.9%. On natural-Let problems it does real damage (30.9 to 16.0). Cut-offs do fall to 17.7% in the Okay group, but those answers simply finish wrong more often, so that's no gain, which is exactly why the method says not to judge by cut-offs.

One signal is worth following. On natural-Here problems Okay reaches 21.4, compared with 13.7 for the original and about 20 for E5. In particular, the strongly-Here bin (margin below -2) gets 37.9 against 24.1 for the original and 27.6 for E5. That's only 29 problems and post hoc, so it proves nothing yet. It does suggest something plausible: problems that strongly prefer the list family may do best staying in that family, in its better opener, which is the group E5 leaves untouched.

I can test that directly, on problems that didn't suggest it. I'll collect the DEV problems E5 keeps in Here, excluding `dev_a1`, and run E9 on just those. If Okay gains at least about 5 points on fresh problems, a three-way policy (strongly-Here to Okay, the rest as E5) is worth building. If it's near zero or negative, the 37.9 was noise and I'll close Okay.
